title: Permutations
description: Generate all orderings of a distinct array using swap-based or used-array backtracking.

data.text: Given an array `nums` of distinct integers, return all possible permutations in any order. A permutation is a reordering where every element appears exactly once.

Treat the array as the permutation being built. At depth `d`, swap each remaining position `i >= d` into position `d`, recurse to `d + 1`, then swap back to restore the array (the backtrack). When `d` reaches the end, the array is a complete permutation. This is in-place and needs no extra `used` bookkeeping.

data.title: Swap-based in-place O(n! * n)

data.text: Build the permutation left-to-right in a separate list, tracking which indices are already used. At each position, try every unused element. This is more verbose but reads clearly and generalizes to permutation-with-duplicates (where you sort and skip repeated choices).

data.title: Used-array O(n! * n)

data.caption: Permutation tree for [1,2,3]: each level fixes one position; there are n! leaves and n * n! total nodes.

data.title: What improved?
data.text: Both are O(n! * n) — the output itself has n! permutations of length n, so that's optimal. Swap-based avoids the `used[]` array and the O(n) `contains` cost, but the used-array version makes duplicate-skipping (permutations II) straightforward.

cards.title: Swap-Based
cards.description: Swap each candidate into the current depth
